triage.name: Common Cold
triage.reason: Extremely common upper respiratory infection with classic history and exam; good for teaching viral URI and antibiotic stewardship.

age.peak: children under 10 and adults with young children at home

demographics: Children average 5–7 colds per year; adults average 2–3
More frequent in households with school-aged children
More common in fall, winter, and early spring in temperate climates

risk_factors.text: Close contact with a person who has a cold
Having young children at home or working in childcare or schools
Crowded indoor settings such as dormitories, barracks, or offices
Touching the face with unwashed hands after contact with contaminated surfaces
Cigarette smoke exposure, including secondhand smoke

social_history: Household members or coworkers with similar symptoms in the past week
exposures: Sick contacts at home, work, or school
Recent air travel or crowded gatherings

chief_complaints.text: My nose is stuffy and running
My throat is scratchy and sore
I have a cough that won't quit
I feel worn down and my head hurts

hpi.onset: Gradual over one to two days, often starting with a scratchy throat or sneezing
hpi.duration: Symptoms peak in 2–3 days and usually resolve within 7–10 days; cough may linger up to 2 weeks
hpi.progression: Sore throat and sneezing come first, then nasal congestion and runny nose build over the next day or two, followed by cough; symptoms then slowly improve
hpi.quality: Scratchy throat, watery then thicker nasal drainage, dry or mildly productive cough
hpi.severity: Mild; annoying but does not keep most people from daily activities
hpi.timing: Continuous through the day, often worse at night when lying down

associated_symptoms.text: Low-grade fever, more often in children

pertinent_negatives: Facial pain or pressure over the sinuses
Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without any improvement
Symptoms that improved and then got worse again

argues_against: Influenza, which typically causes abrupt high fever and severe body aches

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants cannot describe symptoms; they present with fussiness, poor feeding, nasal congestion interfering with feeding, and sometimes fever. Symptoms may last longer than in older children.
Children often have higher fevers than adults and may have more prominent cough and nasal symptoms; they may also develop ear infections or sinusitis as complications.
Fever may be blunted or absent, and symptoms can be milder but complications such as pneumonia are more likely.
Colds can be more severe, last longer, and progress to lower respiratory infection or pneumonia more often.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, speaking in full sentences; may sniffle or wipe nose
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, occasional cough, slightly hoarse voice, no distress
general.severe: Tired-appearing with frequent coughing, but no respiratory distress at rest
general.critical: Not applicable; the common cold does not produce a critical general appearance — if the patient looks toxic or is in respiratory distress, consider another diagnosis

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nasal mucosa with a light and nasal speculum
findings.finding: Erythematous, swollen nasal mucosa with clear to whitish secretions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the nares and ask the patient to sniff
Inspect the posterior pharynx with a tongue blade and light
findings.finding: Mild diffuse erythema of the posterior pharynx without exudate

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tonsils and posterior pharynx
Palpate the anterior and posterior cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: No tender or enlarged cervical lymph nodes
Tympanic membranes pearly gray, translucent, with normal landmarks and mobility

findings.maneuver: Palpate or percuss over the frontal and maxillary sinuses
Auscultate all lung fields anteriorly and posteriorly
findings.finding: Clear breath sounds without crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi

findings.maneuver: Observe respiratory rate and effort at rest
findings.finding: Normal respiratory rate and unlabored breathing

findings.maneuver: Observe for use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, or retractions
findings.finding: No accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, or intercostal retractions

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, including the face and trunk
Flex and rotate the neck passively
findings.finding: Full range of motion without pain or resistance

findings.text: Clear lungs without focal consolidation, infiltrate, or pleural effusion
Mucosal thickening or fluid within the sinuses, which is common in an uncomplicated viral URI and does not by itself indicate bacterial sinusitis
No air-fluid level or complete opacification to suggest bacterial sinusitis

not_indicated.why: The common cold is a clinical diagnosis; a blood count does not change management
Not needed unless the patient is dehydrated or has significant vomiting
Does not distinguish a cold from other viral illnesses or change management
No role in an uncomplicated upper respiratory infection
Not routine for a cold; reserve for influenza-like illness with abrupt high fever and severe body aches
Only if features suggest streptococcal pharyngitis (exudate, tender anterior adenopathy, fever, absence of cough)
Not indicated for an uncomplicated cold; order only if pneumonia is suspected
Not indicated for uncomplicated viral rhinosinusitis; reserve for suspected complications
No role in upper respiratory infection
Not part of the evaluation of an acute cold

decision_points: The common cold is a clinical diagnosis; testing is reserved for patients whose features suggest an alternative or complication
Consider rapid influenza testing when onset is abrupt with high fever and prominent myalgias, especially during influenza season
Consider rapid strep testing or throat culture only when the pharyngitis features suggest group A streptococcus
Consider chest x-ray only when pneumonia is suspected (fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, or focal lung findings)
Consider sinus imaging only when bacterial sinusitis or a complication is suspected, such as symptoms beyond 10 days without improvement, severe symptoms, or double worsening

differential.name: Influenza
differential.why_considered: Viral illness with cough, sore throat, and nasal symptoms
differential.trigger: Abrupt onset with high fever and severe body aches during influenza season

exam: Patient appears more ill than with a cold
labs: Rapid influenza antigen or PCR positive
imaging: Chest x-ray usually normal; may show infiltrates if pneumonia develops

differential.name: COVID-19
differential.why_considered: Viral illness with cough, sore throat, nasal congestion, and fatigue
differential.trigger: Known exposure or loss of taste/smell, or severe systemic symptoms

history: Shortness of breath may be present
exam: Lungs may be clear or show crackles if pneumonia
imaging: Chest x-ray may show bilateral infiltrates in severe cases

differential.name: Acute bacterial sinusitis
differential.why_considered: Nasal congestion, runny nose, and cough can overlap with cold

history: Symptoms lasting >10 days without improvement, or worsening after initial improvement
imaging: CT sinuses shows air-fluid levels or complete opacification

differential.name: Acute bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Prominent cough, often post-viral, can be difficult to distinguish from cold

history: Cough is the predominant symptom, often lasting >5 days
exam: Lungs may have coarse breath sounds or wheezes
imaging: Chest x-ray normal or shows increased bronchovascular markings; no consolidation

differential.name: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis
differential.why_considered: Sore throat is a common cold symptom
differential.trigger: Sore throat with fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and absence of cough

history: Sudden onset of severe sore throat
labs: Rapid strep test or throat culture positive

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: Cough, fever, and malaise can be present in both cold and pneumonia
differential.trigger: Tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal lung findings, or high fever

history: Symptoms may be more severe and prolonged
exam: Crackles or decreased breath sounds focally
imaging: Chest x-ray shows focal consolidation or infiltrate

differential.name: Allergic rhinitis
differential.why_considered: Sneezing, runny nose, and nasal congestion are hallmark symptoms

history: Symptoms triggered by allergens (pollen, dust, pets)
No sore throat or cough typically

severity.mild: Mild nasal congestion, sneezing, scratchy throat, no fever, able to perform daily activities
severity.moderate: Prominent nasal congestion, runny nose, cough, low-grade fever, mild fatigue, some interference with activities
severity.severe: High fever (up to 102°F), significant cough, headache, body aches, feeling quite unwell, but no respiratory distress
severity.critical: Not applicable; the common cold itself is not life-threatening. If a patient appears toxic or in respiratory distress, consider another diagnosis.

red_flags.finding: Shortness of breath at rest or with minimal exertion
red_flags.meaning: Suggests pneumonia or lower respiratory involvement

red_flags.finding: Fever above 102°F or lasting more than 4 days
red_flags.meaning: May indicate a secondary bacterial infection or another diagnosis

red_flags.finding: Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement
red_flags.meaning: Consider bacterial sinusitis or other complication

red_flags.finding: Symptoms that improve then worsen (double worsening)
Severe headache with stiff neck or confusion

red_flags.meaning: Consider pneumonia, tuberculosis, or other serious condition

red_flags.finding: Dehydration (decreased urine output, dry mucous membranes, poor feeding in infants)

complications.name: Acute bacterial sinusitis
clues: Symptoms >10 days without improvement or double worsening

special_populations.differences: Higher fever is common; complications like otitis media and sinusitis are more frequent. Children may have more prominent cough and nasal symptoms. Aspirin should be avoided due to risk of Reye syndrome.
Present with fussiness, poor feeding, nasal congestion interfering with feeding, and fever. Symptoms may last longer. Watch for dehydration and respiratory distress.
Fever may be blunted or absent; symptoms can be milder but complications such as pneumonia are more likely. Monitor for worsening respiratory status.
Colds can be more severe, last longer, and progress to lower respiratory infection or pneumonia more often. Early evaluation and treatment may be needed.

Colds are usually mild, but some over-the-counter medications may not be safe. Acetaminophen is generally preferred for pain and fever. Avoid decongestants and certain cough suppressants unless approved by a provider.

key_questions.question: When did your symptoms start, and how have they changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over 1–2 days, peaking in 2–3 days; duration under 10 days

key_questions.question: What symptoms did you notice first?
key_questions.looking_for: Scratchy throat or sneezing first, then congestion and cough

key_questions.question: How long have the symptoms lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: 7–10 days typical; more than 10 days without improvement suggests bacterial sinusitis

key_questions.question: Did your symptoms improve and then get worse again?
key_questions.looking_for: Double worsening suggests a secondary bacterial infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever? How high, and for how long?
key_questions.looking_for: Low-grade or none; fever above 102°F or lasting more than 4 days suggests another diagnosis

key_questions.question: Are you having any trouble breathing or shortness of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests pneumonia or lower respiratory involvement

key_questions.question: Do you have any pain or pressure over your face or sinuses?
Do you have ear pain or trouble hearing?
How severe is your sore throat? Can you swallow liquids?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild and scratchy with ability to swallow; severe pain or inability to swallow suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you been sick with similar symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts at home, work, school, or daycare

key_questions.question: Do you have asthma, COPD, or any other chronic lung condition?
key_questions.looking_for: Asthma or COPD, which raises the risk of exacerbation or complications

key_questions.question: Do you smoke, or are you exposed to secondhand smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco exposure, which can worsen symptoms and prolong recovery

key_questions.question: What have you taken for your symptoms so far?
key_questions.looking_for: Over-the-counter cold medicines, acetaminophen, or decongestants; check for duplicate ingredients

key_questions.question: Have you had any coughing up of blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests pneumonia, tuberculosis, or another serious condition

key_questions.question: Any severe headache, stiff neck, or confusion?

reasoning_points: Gradual onset of nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and sore throat over 1–2 days
Symptoms peak in 2–3 days and improve within 7–10 days, though cough may linger up to 2 weeks
Low-grade or no fever; absence of high fever, shortness of breath, or focal lung findings
Clear nasal discharge with erythematous, swollen nasal mucosa on exam
Tympanic membranes normal and no sinus tenderness, arguing against otitis media or bacterial sinusitis
Lungs clear without crackles or wheezes and no tachypnea or hypoxemia, arguing against pneumonia
No features suggesting streptococcal pharyngitis (no exudate, no tender anterior adenopathy, cough present)
Diagnosis is clinical; testing and antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated cold

easy: Young adult or school-aged child with classic gradual onset of congestion, runny nose, and sneezing
Clear rhinorrhea and mild pharyngeal erythema on exam
Sick contact at home or school
medium: Patient with prominent cough and postnasal drip where acute bronchitis is considered
Patient with a history of allergic rhinitis and similar recurring symptoms
Low-grade fever in a child with nasal congestion and fussiness
Symptoms at day 8–9 with slow but steady improvement
Patient requesting antibiotics for a cold
hard: Infant with fussiness, poor feeding, and nasal congestion but no classic symptom description
Older adult with blunted fever and mild symptoms where pneumonia must be excluded
Patient with asthma and cough where an exacerbation must be considered
Symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement, raising concern for bacterial sinusitis
Patient with double worsening of symptoms suggesting a secondary bacterial infection
